subject: math
title: Circle
summary: A circle is the set of all points at the same distance from a center. Explore the radius, diameter, circumference, and the special number pi that ties them together.

crossReferences.label: Point (Geometry)
crossReferences.note: The center of a circle is a point, and every rim point is a point too.

crossReferences.label: Segment (Geometry)
crossReferences.note: The radius and diameter are segments inside the circle.

crossReferences.label: Area (Geometry)
crossReferences.note: A circle's area uses pi and the radius squared.

compareCandidate.label: Circle vs. polygon
compareCandidate.description: A polygon is made of straight sides; a circle is one smooth curve where every rim point is the same distance from the center.

plainLanguageExplanation: A circle is every point at exactly the same distance from one center point. The radius is a segment from the center to the rim; the diameter is a segment across through the center — exactly two radii. The distance around the rim is the circumference. For every circle, the circumference divided by the diameter is always the same number: pi (π), about 3.14159. So circumference = 2 × π × radius, or π × diameter. A wheel with radius 1 unit rolls out about 6.28 units per turn.

keyFacts.label: Definition
keyFacts.value: All points the same distance from a center

whyItMatters: Circles are the shape of wheels, planets, coins, and clocks — anything that rolls or orbits. Pi is one of the most famous numbers in math, and understanding circles unlocks measuring anything round.
didYouKnow: The value of pi has been chased for thousands of years — the ancient Babylonians used 3.125 around 1900 BCE, and today computers have calculated trillions of digits, yet the decimal never repeats and never ends.
compareReason: Students expect all shapes to have straight sides — comparing the smooth circle with a four-sided polygon shows what makes it unique.
